title: Cap. IX: Roses vs stones; tithes harmless, Adam's sin supreme evil — before Responsio 2
pass_a_gloss: If someone throws roses at a passer-by, nothing absurd follows, for roses barely harm. Does it follow likewise that if someone throws stones or mud at a passer-by, nothing absurd follows? Paying tithes stands like a rose that could not harm Levi; but Adam's sin stands not only like a stone but like the supreme evil. So it need not be alien to justice if Abraham's payment of tithes is attributed to Levi, because it neither harmed him nor could harm him. Does it follow that it is not alien to justice if the sin Adam committed is attributed to his posterity and so the greatest evil is inflicted on them? Other answers are scarcely needed; yet Garissoles assigns Placeus four further replies, perhaps drawn from what he calls the Prior Manuscript, and tries at great length to refute them — unhappily, as is his way. Placeus stops the opening block here before entering Responsio secunda.
pass_b_english: If someone throws roses at a passer-by, nothing absurd will follow: for these barely harm. Does it follow likewise that if someone throws stones or mud at a passer-by, nothing absurd will follow? But the payment of tithes stands as a rose that could not harm Levi; Adam's sin, however, stands not only as a stone, but as the supreme evil. It will not therefore have been alien to justice if the payment of tithes made by Abraham is attributed to Levi, because it neither harmed him nor could harm him. Does it follow from that that it is not alien to justice if the sin committed by Adam is attributed to his posterity, and so the greatest evil is inflicted on them? There is not much need of other replies; yet D. Garissoles assigns us four others, which he perhaps drew out of what he calls the Prior Manuscript, and tries at great length to refute — but, after his manner, with an unhappy attempt.
source_text: Si quis in praetereuntem rosas projiciat, nihil sequetur absurdi: hae enim minime nocent. An ergo similiter, si quis in praetereuntem lapides aut lutum projiciat, nihil sequetur absurdi? Se habet autem solutio decimarum ut rosa quae non potuit nocere Levi: At peccatum Adami non solum ut lapis, sed ut summum malum. Non fuerit igitur alienum a justitia, si solutio decimarum ab Abrahamo facta tribuatur Levi; quia id ei nullo modo nocuit, aut nocere potuit: An sequitur inde, non esse alienum a justitia, si peccatum ab Adamo commissum ejus posteris tribuatur, atque ita malum maximum illis inferatur? Non admodum opus est aliis responsionibus; quatuor tamen alias nobis D. Garissolius tribuit, quas fortasse ex Priore, quod vocat, Manuscripto exprompsit, & prolixe admodum refellere conatur, sed, pro suo more, conatu infoelici.
